item.title: Airbnb Requirements in Medellín: Building Rules, the New POT and RNT (2026)
item.description: What you need to rent on Airbnb in Medellín in 2026: building bylaws, the new POT zones, RNT, police notice, TRA and SIRE. Checklist and table inside.
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: to rent an apartment on Airbnb in Medellín you need at least five things: land-use rules at your address that allow tourist homes, building bylaws (reglamento de propiedad horizontal) that expressly authorize it, an active National Tourism Registry (RNT), a written notice to the nearest police station, and a record of every guest (TRA, plus SIRE for foreigners). Miss any one of them and the city can suspend the rental, even if your RNT is up to date.

This guide, current as of November 2026, focuses on the two requirements that stop the most deals right now: building bylaws and the new POT (Medellín's land-use plan). For a full walkthrough of the RNT, TRA and SIRE, read Is Airbnb legal in Medellín? RNT, TRA and SIRE explained. This is general information, not legal or tax advice. We are not lawyers or tax advisors, so for your specific case consult a qualified professional and confirm with the relevant authority.

What are the requirements to rent on Airbnb in Medellín?

The Alcaldía de Medellín summarizes the rules in its tourist-home infographic (Spanish) and its Q&A What is allowed and what is not. Here is the full list, in the order we suggest checking it:

#RequirementWhat it isWhere to check or apply
1Land use (POT)Your address must be in a zone that allows tourist lodgingAlcaldía de Medellín (POT land-use rules)
2Building bylawsThe reglamento de propiedad horizontal must expressly authorize tourist homesBuilding administration and the property's title certificate
3RNTNational Tourism Registry; free, renewed every year between 1 January and 31 Marchrnt.confecamaras.co
4Police noticeWritten notice of opening to the commander of the nearest police stationLocal police station
5TRAAccommodation registration card for every guestMinCIT system
6SIREReporting of foreign guestsMigración Colombia
7RUTTax registration of the operatorDIAN

Items 4 to 6 come from Article 87 of Colombia's National Police and Coexistence Code (Law 1801 of 2016), according to the city's infographic. The Alcaldía also stresses a point many foreign owners miss: the RNT does not replace land-use rules. You need both.

What does Medellín's new POT say about short-term rentals?

Medellín's City Council approved the revised land-use plan (Plan de Ordenamiento Territorial, POT) in its second debate in the early hours of 5 November 2026, with 18 votes in favor, as reported by Minuto30. According to the Alcaldía's explainer Tourist homes and the POT: where yes, where no, the plan does not ban short-term rentals citywide. It sorts them by zone:

  • Low-mix zones (mainly residential): tourist homes are restricted.
  • Medium-mix zones: allowed only near transport corridors such as the Metro.
  • High-mix zones: allowed.

Outlets such as RCN Radio mention parts of El Poblado, Laureles and Belén among the areas where tourist homes could operate, but stress that not every property in those neighborhoods qualifies: the exact address matters, not the neighborhood name. Agencia PI reports that lodgings already operating with all requirements in place could continue.

Watch the dates: as of 13 November 2026, the sources we checked said the agreement was going to the mayor for signature and the final text was not yet public (ORP Urbanismo). Before you buy or furnish a unit for short-term rental, get the land-use status of the exact address and read the official text once it is published.

Does my building have to allow Airbnb in its bylaws?

Yes. Decree 1836 of 2021, which regulates tourist-home providers, requires that when a property is under the horizontal property regime (almost every apartment building and gated complex), the bylaws must expressly authorize tourist-home use. Bylaws that simply do not forbid it are not enough. The same decree requires building administrators to report units used as tourist homes to the Vice Ministry of Tourism.

How to check the bylaws in 4 steps

  1. Ask the building administration for the current reglamento, including every amendment.
  2. Find the section on the use of private units. The words that matter are vivienda turística, alojamiento turístico or arrendamiento por días. If it only says "residential use" or "family housing", there is no express authorization.
  3. Check the property's title certificate (certificado de tradición y libertad) to confirm any amendment was registered.
  4. Ask the administration whether other units are already reported as tourist homes and which house rules apply (visitor registration, common areas, move-ins).

What if the bylaws don't allow it?

The only route is to amend them. Under Article 46 of Law 675 of 2001, amending the bylaws requires a qualified majority of 70% of the ownership coefficients, counted over the whole building rather than only those present at the meeting, as Gerencie explains. The amendment is then recorded in a public deed and registered with the public registry office. In practice, reaching 70% in a building where most owners live on site can be hard. If you are buying for Airbnb income, buy where the authorization already exists; do not plan on changing it later.

What happens if you operate without meeting the requirements?

The Alcaldía describes the consequences of informal operation: suspension of the activity, fines and proceedings that can end in closure. The city reports that between January 2024 and 18 September 2026 it carried out 408 inspections and imposed 105 suspensions for breaches of Article 87. Separately, as we explain in our RNT guide, Law 2068 of 2020 provides for platforms to remove listings without an active RNT when the authorities ask.

Is the RNT about to change?

Possibly. In July 2026 MinCIT published a draft decree that would, among other changes, require a separate RNT for each tourist home. As of November 2026 we found no confirmation that it has been issued. Keep renewing your RNT between 1 January and 31 March, and check the decree's status before the 2027 renewal.

Checklist before you list

  • Land-use status of the address under the current POT.
  • Building bylaws with express, registered authorization.
  • RUT with DIAN.
  • Active RNT, with the number shown on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia or VRBO.
  • Written notice to the nearest police station.
  • A process for TRA and SIRE on every booking.
  • A reminder to renew the RNT (1 January to 31 March).

How we help

Medellín Concierge manages RNT, SIRE and TRA compliance and offers full Airbnb management in Medellín: dynamic pricing, 24/7 guest communication, cleaning and maintenance, and an owner portal with monthly financial statements. If your building or zone does not allow short-term rentals, we also offer property management in Colombia for long-term leases. For the big picture, read our Medellín property management guide or visit our home page for property management in Medellín.

Want to know whether your apartment, or the one you plan to buy, can legally operate as a short-term rental? Request a free consultation and we will review it with you. You can see our fees in the plans section.

FAQ

Can I rent on Airbnb in Medellín if the building bylaws say nothing about it?

No. Under Decree 1836 of 2021, buildings under horizontal property must expressly authorize tourist-home use in their bylaws. Silence is not authorization.

Does an RNT let me operate anywhere in Medellín?

No. The Alcaldía states that the RNT does not replace land-use rules. Under the new POT, approved by the City Council in November 2026 and not yet officially published when this guide was written, tourist homes are restricted in low-mix residential zones.

What vote does a building need to allow Airbnb?

Amending the bylaws requires 70% of the ownership coefficients under Article 46 of Law 675 of 2001, followed by a public deed and registration. For your specific case, consult a qualified professional.

Last reviewed: November 2026. General information, not legal or tax advice. Regulations change: confirm with the relevant authority or a qualified professional.

item.title: Airbnb vs Long-Term Rental in Medellín: Which Is Right for Your Property?
item.description: Airbnb or a long-term lease in Medellín? Compare the rules (RNT, building permission, POT), income, costs and workload with our table and checklist.
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: neither option wins for every owner. Short-term rental (Airbnb and similar platforms) can earn more per night, but it needs an RNT registration, explicit permission in the building's rules (reglamento de propiedad horizontal), a location where land-use rules allow it, and hands-on daily operations. A traditional long-term lease gives steadier income with far less work, under the clear rules of Law 820 of 2003. In Medellín today, the deciding question is usually whether your building and your zone allow tourist rentals at all.

This guide is current as of November 2026 and gives you a comparison table and a checklist. It is general information: rules change, so confirm the details for your property, and for tax or legal questions consult a qualified professional (we are not tax or legal advisors).

What is the difference between short-term and long-term rentals in Medellín?

  • Short-term rental ("vivienda turística"): stays by the night or week, usually through Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia or VRBO. Colombia treats this as a tourism service, so it requires the National Tourism Registry (RNT), reporting foreign guests to Migración Colombia (SIRE) and the hotel registration card (TRA). We explain each step in Is Airbnb legal in Medellín? RNT, TRA and SIRE.
  • Long-term rental ("arriendo de vivienda urbana"): one tenant, usually on a lease of a year or more, governed by Law 820 of 2003. Among other things, the rent can only rise every 12 months and by no more than 100% of the previous year's CPI (Article 20). See our guide to long-term rental management in Medellín.

Does my building and neighborhood allow Airbnb?

Ask this before you look at returns. In its Q&A ¿Qué está permitido y qué no?, the Medellín mayor's office (Alcaldía) explains that:

  1. In apartment buildings and gated complexes, tourist rental must be expressly authorized in the building's horizontal-property rules.
  2. The RNT does not replace land-use rules. According to the Alcaldía, Article 87 of the Police Code requires both.

Enforcement is also stepping up. According to the Alcaldía de Medellín, there were 408 inspections of tourist homes between 2024 and 2026 to date, and 105 were temporarily suspended for breaking the rules. Tourist-home operators registered in the RNT grew from 521 in 2019 to 8,322 in 2026.

The city's land-use plan (POT) revision is redrawing the map too. Press reports from early November 2026 say the City Council approved the revision in its second debate (see RCN Radio and, on the earlier process, Publimetro). The Alcaldía says in Vivienda turística y POT: dónde sí, dónde no that the plan does not ban the activity but concentrates it in mixed-use zones and areas near metro stations, with restrictions in mainly residential, low-mix zones. We had not seen the final published text when we wrote this, so check your exact address before you buy or convert.

Comparison table: Airbnb vs long-term rental

FactorShort-term (Airbnb)Long-term lease
IncomeVariable: depends on season, occupancy and nightly rateFixed monthly rent; yearly increase capped at CPI (Law 820, Art. 20)
RegistrationsRNT, SIRE, TRA and building authorizationLease contract; third-party managers must follow Law 820 rules
LocationOnly where land use allows it (2026 POT revision)Allowed in residential zones
OperationsDaily: messages, check-ins, cleaning, maintenance, reviewsLight: rent collection, inspections, occasional repairs
FurnishingFully furnished and equipped for guestsFurnished or unfurnished
Main riskFines or suspension if you operate without the requirements; low-season monthsLate payment and empty months between tenants
FlexibilityYou can block dates for your own visitsThe unit is occupied for the whole lease

Which earns more in Medellín?

It depends. Press analyses such as Portafolio's and Bancolombia's blog agree that short-term rental can out-earn a traditional lease, in exchange for more management and more requirements. It also carries more costs: cleaning, utilities, internet, platform fees, replacing linens and supplies, and management. We don't publish yield figures, because they vary widely by neighborhood, building and unit type.

To compare with real numbers, run this exercise for your own unit:

  • Short-term: expected nightly rate × booked nights per year, minus platform fees, cleaning, utilities, supplies, management and taxes.
  • Long-term: monthly rent × 12, minus expected empty months, management, maintenance and taxes.
  • Compare net, not gross, and count the time you (or your manager) will spend on each.

We are happy to run these numbers with you. You can see what our Airbnb management in Medellín covers on that page, and our management fees on our plans.

Checklist: which option fits you?

Tick the ones that apply:

  • The building rules expressly allow tourist rentals.
  • The address is in a zone where land use allows tourist accommodation.
  • You can get the RNT and keep up with SIRE and TRA (or hand them to a manager).
  • The unit is furnished, or you are willing to invest in furnishing, photos and a listing.
  • You prefer higher income even if it varies month to month.
  • You want to use the property yourself a few weeks a year.

If you ticked nearly all of them, short-term rental may make sense. If either of the first two fails, the realistic option today is a long-term lease (or a furnished monthly rental under whatever rules apply; check with a qualified professional).

Can I switch from Airbnb to a long-term lease, or the other way round?

Yes, but plan it. Moving to a long-term lease means following Law 820's rules on lease length, renewal and termination. Moving to short-term means confirming building rules and land use first, then getting the RNT. Either way, review the tax side with an accountant.

How Medellín Concierge can help

We provide property management in Medellín for both models:

  • Short-term: listing management on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO, dynamic pricing, 24/7 guest communication, cleaning and maintenance, and RNT, SIRE and TRA compliance management. More on Airbnb management in Medellín.
  • Long-term: management for owners living in Colombia or abroad. More on property management in Colombia.
  • Both: styling, photos and listings to launch your property, an owner portal with monthly GAAP financial statements.

For the bigger picture, read our complete Medellín property management guide.

Not sure which is right for you? Request a free consultation and we will look at your building, your zone and your numbers together.

FAQ

Is it legal to run an Airbnb in Medellín?

Yes, if you meet the requirements: a valid RNT, SIRE reporting, TRA, express authorization in the building rules and land use that allows it, according to the Alcaldía de Medellín (as of November 2026). The POT revision may change where it is allowed, so check your exact address.

How much can long-term rent go up each year?

As of November 2026, Law 820 of 2003 (Article 20) lets the landlord raise the rent every 12 months by up to 100% of the previous year's CPI, which DANE publishes.

What happens if I run an Airbnb without an RNT?

You risk sanctions. Law 2068 of 2020 requires platforms not to publish, or to remove, listings without a registration, and the Alcaldía has suspended tourist homes for violations. For your specific case, consult a lawyer.

item.title: How to Choose a Property Manager in Medellín: A Checklist for Owners
item.description: What to verify before you hire a property manager or inmobiliaria in Medellín: registrations, fees, reports, contracts and red flags. Owner checklist.
item.content:encoded:
Handing your apartment to someone else is a big decision, especially if you live abroad and will rarely see the property in person. In Medellín you can choose between a traditional real estate agency (inmobiliaria), an Airbnb co-host, an independent manager or a full-service management company. They are not the same thing, and the right choice depends on how you plan to rent.

This checklist walks you through what to verify before you sign, which questions to ask, and which warning signs to take seriously. It reflects the rules as of November 2026; regulations change, so confirm the details with the relevant authority or a qualified professional before you decide. For the bigger picture, start with our Medellín property management guide.

Step 1: Decide what you actually need managed

Before you compare companies, be clear about the rental model:

  • Long-term lease (arriendo de vivienda). One tenant, usually for a year or more, under Colombia's urban housing lease law, Law 820 of 2003. The manager's job is tenant screening, the contract, rent collection, annual increases and maintenance.
  • Short-term or tourist rental (vivienda turística). Stays of less than 30 days on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia or VRBO. Here the manager also handles pricing, guest messages, check-ins, cleaning and the tourism registrations. Our post on whether Airbnb is legal in Medellín explains the RNT, TRA and SIRE in detail.
  • Both, or not sure yet. Some owners start with one model and switch later. A manager that offers both can help you compare honestly.

Many traditional inmobiliarias focus on long-term leases, while many co-hosts focus only on short stays. Ask each candidate which model they actually run day to day.

Step 2: Verify the company is legally set up

These checks are free and take a few minutes. A professional manager should be glad you asked.

  1. Business registration. Colombian companies are registered with their local Chamber of Commerce and appear in the national business registry, RUES. Search the company name or NIT and confirm it is active.
  2. Landlord registration (matrícula de arrendador) for long-term leases. Under Article 28 of Law 820 of 2003, people and companies whose main activity is renting out urban housing, their own or other people's, or brokering leases must register with the municipality. Decree 51 of 2004 (text on Función Pública) adds that they must register in every municipality where they operate and show their registration number when they advertise. In Medellín the process is run by the Alcaldía (official page). Ask for the number; if they also manage in Envigado or Sabaneta, ask about those municipalities too.
  3. National Tourism Registry (RNT) for short-term rentals. Tourist rentals and the companies that operate them must be registered in the RNT, which is run by MinCIT through the chambers of commerce. You can look up a registration on the public RNT search. Check that it is active and current, not just that a number exists: national authorities have filed charges against tourist-rental operators working without a valid RNT (Portafolio).

The Alcaldía de Medellín itself has urged people to check the legality and track record of real estate agencies before handing over money (Minuto30). That advice applies just as much to owners as to tenants.

Step 3: Ask how your money moves

This is where good and bad managers differ most. Ask:

  • Where is rent or booking income deposited, and when is it paid to you? Is it kept separate from the company's own money?
  • What exactly do the fees cover, and what is charged on top (cleaning, repairs, restocking, listing setup, lease renewals)? Ask for the full fee schedule in writing.
  • What reports will you receive? Monthly statements should show every income and expense line so you can check them against bank deposits.
  • Who approves repairs, and up to what amount can the manager spend without asking you?

If you live abroad, also ask how payments reach you and in which currency (see our guide to managing a Colombian property from abroad). For tax questions about rental income, consult a qualified Colombian accountant; a property manager is not a tax advisor.

Step 4: Check operations, not just the sales pitch

A polished website is easy; reliable operations are not. Questions worth asking:

  • Who answers guests or tenants at 2 a.m.? Is there 24/7 coverage, and in which languages?
  • Who cleans and inspects the unit, and how are damages documented between stays or at move-out?
  • How do they work with your building's administration? Many Medellín buildings (propiedad horizontal) have their own rules on tourist stays, visitors and moves. A manager should know your building's reglamento before listing anything.
  • For short stays: how are guests reported? Hosts must report foreign guests to Migración Colombia through SIRE and register stays in the TRA. Ask who does it and how quickly.
  • For long leases: how are tenants screened and what guarantee is used, such as a co-signer or a lease insurance policy?

Step 5: Read the management contract carefully

Before you sign, look for:

  • Term and exit. How long is the contract, how much notice is needed to end it, and are there exit fees?
  • Who owns the listing and the reviews. If you leave, can your Airbnb listing and its history stay with you?
  • Insurance and liability. Who pays if a guest or tenant damages the unit?
  • Scope in writing. Every service you were promised verbally should appear in the contract.

Have a Colombian lawyer review any contract you are unsure about. We can explain how management works in practice, but we do not give legal advice.

Red flags to take seriously

  • No company registration, or a registration that does not match the name on the contract.
  • They cannot give you a matrícula number (long-term) or an active RNT (short-term).
  • Vague fees, or "we'll sort it out later" when you ask about costs.
  • No written monthly statements, or payments to personal accounts.
  • Guaranteed income promises with no explanation of how they were calculated.
  • Pressure to sign the same day.

How Medellín Concierge approaches it

At Medellín Concierge we manage both short-term rentals on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO and long-term leases in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta. We handle RNT, SIRE and TRA registrations, dynamic pricing, 24/7 guest communication, cleaning and maintenance, and styling, photos and listings to launch your property. Owners get an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements, and our plans and fees are published on our plans page.

Use this checklist on us too: ask us every question above. Learn more about our property management in Medellín or our Airbnb management in Medellín, and meet the people behind it on our team page.

Comparing managers for your Medellín apartment? Request a free consultation and we will answer your checklist, point by point, for your property.

FAQ

Does a property manager in Medellín need a license?

As of November 2026, there is no single "property manager license", but there are registrations. Companies whose main activity is renting out or brokering urban housing must hold a matrícula de arrendador in each municipality where they operate (Law 820 of 2003 and Decree 51 of 2004), and tourist rentals must be in the RNT. Ask for both numbers and verify them.

How do I check if a Medellín real estate agency is legitimate?

Look up the company in RUES, ask for its matrícula de arrendador number (it should appear in its ads), check any RNT number on the public RNT search, and get the fee schedule and contract in writing before you hand over keys or money.

Should I choose an inmobiliaria or an Airbnb manager?

It depends on your rental model. For a long-term tenant, look for experience with Law 820 leases (see our long-term rental management guide); for short stays, look for RNT, guest reporting and 24/7 operations. If you are undecided, our Medellín property management guide compares both models.

item.title: Long-Term Rental Management in Medellín: What Owners Need to Know
item.description: Rent increases capped by IPC (5.10% for 2026), no cash deposits, notice rules and what a manager handles: a plain guide to long-term rentals in Medellín.
item.content:encoded:
Not every Medellín apartment belongs on Airbnb. Some buildings do not allow tourist stays, some owners prefer one steady tenant over a stream of guests, and some simply want fewer moving parts while they live abroad. A long-term lease (an arriendo) can be a good fit, but it comes with its own rulebook in Colombia, and that rulebook favors careful paperwork.

This guide explains, in plain language, the rules that shape long-term rental management in Medellín as of November 2026: how rent increases work, what you can and cannot ask a tenant for, how a lease ends, and what a property manager typically handles. It is general information, not legal advice. Rules change, so confirm the details for your property before you sign anything.

Long-term vs short-term: two different rulebooks

In Colombia, a short-term tourist rental (vivienda turística) is a stay of less than 30 days under Decree 1836 of 2021. It needs an active National Tourism Registry (RNT) from MinCIT, guest reporting, and a building and land use that allow tourist stays.

A long-term residential lease follows a different law: Law 820 of 2003, the national framework for urban housing leases. It sets how rent can rise, what guarantees are allowed, and how either side can end the contract. If you are still deciding between the two models, our Medellín property management guide compares them side by side.

How much can you raise the rent?

This is the question owners ask most, and Law 820 answers it clearly:

  • Once a year. The rent can be increased only after each 12 months of the contract, counted from the start date or from the last legal increase.
  • Capped by inflation. The increase cannot exceed the consumer price index (IPC) of the previous calendar year, as Portafolio's guide to rent increases explains. Owner and tenant can agree on a smaller increase.

For leases renewing in 2026, the reference is 2025 inflation. DANE reported that the IPC closed 2025 at 5.10% (Portafolio, Noticias Caracol). So a residential lease that reaches its anniversary in 2026 can generally rise by up to 5.10%. The 2027 cap will depend on the 2026 inflation figure, which DANE publishes in early January.

Commercial leases (offices, shops) are not under this cap. If you own a mixed-use property, check which rules apply to each contract.

Deposits: why they are different in Colombia

Owners coming from the US, Canada or Europe often expect to collect a cash security deposit. For urban residential leases, Article 16 of Law 820 does not allow it: landlords cannot require cash deposits or other real guarantees (cauciones reales) to secure the tenant's obligations, as the Bogotá Hábitat landlord guide summarizes.

Instead, Colombian leases usually rely on personal guarantees: a co-signer (codeudor or fiador) or a rental guarantee policy (póliza de arrendamiento) from an insurer. Which option is available, and how strong it is, depends on the tenant and the insurer. This is one of the main reasons screening matters so much in long-term rentals here.

How a long-term lease ends

Ending a lease is where informal arrangements cause the most trouble. A few points from Law 820, as explained in this CMS Law analysis and the Constitutional Court's ruling C-426 of 2023:

  • Written notice matters. If the required written notice is not given, the contract generally renews automatically for the same term.
  • Ending during an extension has a cost. During the contract's extensions, the landlord can end it unilaterally with at least three months' written notice and an indemnity equal to three months' rent, deposited in favor of the tenant under the procedure in Article 23.
  • Other grounds exist, such as needing the property for the owner's own home, major works or a sale, each with its own notice and conditions.

These steps are formal. Missing a date or sending notice the wrong way can extend a lease you meant to end. For any specific termination, talk to a Colombian lawyer first.

Do you need to register as a landlord?

Article 28 of Law 820 created a landlord registry (matrícula de arrendadores). Under the regulation now compiled in Decree 1077 of 2015, it applies to people or companies that, as owners or sublessors, hold more than five lease contracts, on their own properties or third parties' (Decree 51 of 2004, Función Pública). The registration itself has no cost.

In Medellín, the Alcaldía handles it as an official procedure: see the city's Matrícula de arrendadores page. An owner renting one or two apartments directly is usually below the threshold, but confirm your own case with the Alcaldía.

What a long-term property manager typically handles

Day to day, long-term rental management in Medellín usually covers:

  1. Preparing the unit. Repairs, cleaning, and photos and a listing that show the apartment well.
  2. Finding and screening tenants. Checking income, references and the guarantee (co-signer or rental policy) before a lease is signed.
  3. The lease and the inventory. A written contract and a detailed move-in inventory with photos, so the move-out comparison is clear.
  4. Rent and building fees. Tracking monthly rent and the building's administration fee (cuota de administración), and following up on late payments.
  5. Maintenance. Coordinating repairs with trusted vendors and the building administration.
  6. Annual increases and renewals. Applying the IPC increase on the right date and sending notices on time.
  7. Reporting. Clear monthly numbers so you know what the property earned and spent.

If you live outside Colombia, the last three items are the hardest to do from a distance, and the ones where missed dates cost the most.

How Medellín Concierge can help

At Medellín Concierge we offer long-term property management alongside short-term rental management, so you can choose the model that fits your building and your goals, and switch later if the rules or your plans change. Owners get an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements. We also handle cleaning and maintenance, and styling, photos and listings to launch your property, in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta.

Learn more about our property management in Medellín, and see plans and fees at /#plans. We are not tax or legal advisors: for contracts, evictions or taxes on rental income, consult a qualified Colombian lawyer or accountant.

Thinking about a long-term tenant for your Medellín apartment? Request a free consultation and we will walk you through the options for your property.

FAQ

How much can I raise the rent on a long-term lease in Medellín in 2026?

For residential leases, the increase is limited to the previous year's IPC and can be applied once every 12 months. DANE reported 2025 inflation at 5.10%, so leases reaching their anniversary in 2026 can generally rise by up to that amount. Owner and tenant can agree on less.

Can I ask a tenant in Colombia for a security deposit?

Not a cash deposit for a residential lease: Article 16 of Law 820 of 2003 prohibits cash deposits and real guarantees. Owners usually use a co-signer (codeudor) or a rental guarantee policy instead.

Is long-term or short-term rental better for my Medellín apartment?

It depends on your building's rules, the land use, the neighborhood and how hands-on you want to be. Short-term rentals need an RNT and guest reporting; long-term leases follow Law 820. Our Medellín property management guide compares both, and we are happy to look at your specific property.

item.title: El Poblado vs Laureles vs Envigado: Where to Stay in Medellín for a Month
item.description: El Poblado, Laureles or Envigado? Compare where to stay in Medellín for a month: vibe, noise, Metro access and what to check before booking.
item.content:encoded:
A month in Medellín is long enough to live like a local and short enough that the wrong neighborhood can spoil it. Most visitors who come for 30 days or more end up choosing between three areas: El Poblado, Laureles and Envigado. They are close on a map but feel very different day to day. This guide compares them for a month-long stay, for remote workers, slow travellers and people testing the city before a longer move, so you can pick the one that fits how you actually live.

This is general information as of November 2026. Neighborhoods change, and so do transport and immigration rules, so check the latest before you book.

The quick answer

  • El Poblado: best if you want restaurants, cafés, nightlife and English-friendly services within walking distance, and you don't mind a busier, more touristic area.
  • Laureles: best if you want a calmer, flatter, more residential neighborhood with a local feel, while still being well connected.
  • Envigado: best if you want quiet everyday life, value space and routine over nightlife, and are happy to travel a bit further for the city's main attractions.

Many travel and expat guides describe a common pattern: start in El Poblado, then move to Laureles or Envigado once you know the city (Expat Exchange, Medellin Guru). For a single month, it makes sense to choose the area that matches your daily routine from day one.

How the three areas fit together

It helps to know what each name actually refers to. According to the Alcaldía de Medellín, the city's urban area is divided into 16 comunas. El Poblado is Comuna 14 and Laureles-Estadio is Comuna 11, so both are part of Medellín itself. Envigado is different: it is a separate municipality just south of Medellín, part of the Valle de Aburrá metropolitan area (La FM). In practice the cities run into each other, and you will hardly notice the border.

El Poblado: the most convenient first base

El Poblado sits on the hillside in the southeast of the city. It has the highest concentration of hotels, restaurants, coworking spaces and shopping malls, and areas such as Parque Lleras and Provenza are known for their nightlife. For a first-time visitor, that means almost everything is close and many businesses are used to serving foreigners.

Good for a month if you:

  • want to walk to cafés, gyms and restaurants every day;
  • are new to Colombia and want services in English nearby;
  • enjoy going out in the evening.

Think twice if you:

  • are sensitive to noise, especially near the nightlife streets on weekends;
  • want flat streets for walking or cycling (much of El Poblado is steep);
  • are on a tight budget: guides consistently describe it as the most expensive area of the city (Expat Exchange).

Getting around: Metro Line A has stations at Poblado and Aguacatala along the river at the bottom of the hill (El Colombiano). Higher up the hill, most people use taxis or ride apps.

Laureles: the local favourite for longer stays

Laureles-Estadio lies west of the river and is mostly flat, with tree-lined streets, circular avenues and lower buildings than El Poblado. Expat guides often single it out for month-long and longer stays because it combines a residential, local feel with plenty of cafés, restaurants and parks (Medellin Guru). The area around the Atanasio Girardot sports complex and the shopping centres near it add everyday convenience.

Good for a month if you:

  • work remotely and want a calmer routine;
  • like walking or cycling on flat streets;
  • want to practise your Spanish and live among Colombian neighbours.

Think twice if you:

  • want nightlife on your doorstep every night (there is some, but less than in El Poblado);
  • will spend most evenings in El Poblado, since crossing the city can take a while at rush hour.

Getting around: Metro Line B serves the area, with Estadio station close to the Unicentro and Obelisco shopping centres (Metro de Medellín). Line B connects with Line A in the city centre.

Envigado: quiet, residential and practical

Envigado has its own centre, main park, markets and services, and many parts of it feel like a small town inside the metropolitan area. It is generally less touristic than El Poblado, which is exactly why some long-stay visitors choose it. Because it lies south of Medellín, the trip to the city's main sights is longer, so it suits people who are here to live and work, not to tick off attractions.

Good for a month if you:

  • want quiet nights and a neighbourhood routine;
  • prefer local markets and family-run restaurants;
  • need a calm place to work and only go into Medellín now and then.

Think twice if you:

  • want to go out often in El Poblado or the city centre;
  • will be sightseeing most days.

Getting around: Metro Line A continues south through Ayurá and Envigado stations, so you can reach Poblado station in a few stops without changing lines.

A note on transport

The Metro is the backbone of public transport in the Valle de Aburrá, but like any rail system it has occasional closures and works. Local media have reported temporary interruptions on parts of Line A in the south of the valley, for example after damage to the track between Poblado and Aguacatala stations (El Colombiano). Before you choose an apartment because of a nearby station, check the current status on the Metro de Medellín's official channels.

How long can you stay as a visitor?

A month fits comfortably within a standard visitor stay for most nationalities, but it is worth checking before you plan a longer trip. Colombia's migration authority, Migración Colombia, sets the rules for entry and stay permits, and they are updated from time to time (Resolución 0599 de 2026, Cancillería normograma). Requirements depend on your nationality, so confirm yours with Migración Colombia or the Cancillería before you travel. This is general information, not immigration advice.

What to check before booking a monthly rental

Whichever neighborhood you choose, the same checklist applies:

  1. Exact location, not just the neighborhood name. A street can be quiet or noisy, steep or flat.
  2. Internet speed if you work online. Ask for a recent speed test.
  3. What the price includes: utilities, internet, building fees (administración) and cleaning.
  4. Noise: ask whether the unit faces a busy street or a nightlife area.
  5. The contract: the dates, the deposit, if any, and the cancellation terms in writing.
  6. Registration: legal short-term rentals in Colombia are registered in the National Tourism Registry (RNT), which you can ask the host about.

Ready to find your place?

If you already know which neighborhood suits you, browse our furnished rentals in Medellín and ask us about dates and availability. You book directly with us, and we can tell you about the building, the street and what is included before you commit.

Own an apartment in one of these neighborhoods? Read our Medellín property management guide or learn more about property management in Medellín with Medellín Concierge, and request a free consultation.

FAQ

Which is the best neighborhood in Medellín for a one-month stay? It depends on your routine. El Poblado is the most convenient for nightlife and services, Laureles is calmer and popular with remote workers, and Envigado is the quietest and most residential.

Is Envigado part of Medellín? No. Envigado is a separate municipality next to Medellín, within the Valle de Aburrá metropolitan area. It is connected to Medellín by Metro Line A.

Can I stay a month in Medellín as a tourist? For many nationalities a one-month visit fits within a standard visitor stay, but rules depend on your nationality and change from time to time. Check with Migración Colombia before you travel.

item.title: Managing a Colombian Property From Abroad: RNT, SIRE and Getting Paid
item.description: Own a Medellín apartment but live abroad? What to keep in order: RNT, TRA and SIRE guest reporting, foreign investment, taxes and getting paid.
item.content:encoded:
Owning an apartment in Medellín while living in Miami, Madrid or Toronto is common, and it can work very well. But distance changes the job. You cannot walk over to meet a guest, check a leak or sign a form at the notary. This guide explains, in plain language, what an owner abroad needs to keep in order: the registrations (RNT, TRA and SIRE), the paperwork around foreign money and taxes, and how to see and receive your income.

Everything below is general information as of November 2026. Rules in Colombia change often, especially for short-term rentals, so confirm the current requirements with us or with the authority before you act. For tax and legal questions, speak with a qualified Colombian accountant or lawyer; we are not tax or legal advisors.

First decision: short-term or long-term?

The obligations depend on how you rent.

  • Short-term (tourist) rentals, such as Airbnb or Booking.com stays, are treated as vivienda turística: a tourism service with its own registrations and guest reporting.
  • Long-term rentals (arriendos of months or years) follow ordinary lease rules and do not need tourism registrations, but they still need a written contract, rent collection, maintenance and someone to deal with the tenant.

Our Medellín property management guide compares both models in detail. The rest of this post focuses on the extra layers that matter when you are not in the country.

The RNT: your tourism registration

If you rent to tourists, the property must be listed in the Registro Nacional de Turismo (RNT). Registration is free and done online through the Confecámaras RNT system, and it must be renewed every year. The Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism (MinCIT) reminds providers that anyone who is not registered, or does not renew, cannot legally provide tourism services.

The requirements for tourist homes are set out in Decreto 1836 de 2021, as MinCIT explains in this 2026 answer to a citizen request. Two points catch many owners by surprise:

  1. Your building has to allow it. The building's rules (reglamento de propiedad horizontal) must permit tourist use.
  2. The RNT is not the same as land-use permission. The Alcaldía de Medellín explains that the RNT is a tourism registration and does not replace land-use (uso del suelo) compliance; both are required. Its November 2026 infographic for tourist homes tells owners to check that the property sits in a zone where the land use is compatible with the activity.

The sector has grown fast. According to the Alcaldía, the number of tourist-home providers registered in the RNT in Medellín went from 521 in 2019 to 8,322 in 2026 (source). With that growth has come more regulation: the city is revising where tourist homes can operate as part of its land-use plan (POT) (Alcaldía de Medellín), and national changes to the RNT have been discussed in the press (El Colombiano). If you are abroad, this is the area most worth having someone watch for you.

TRA and SIRE: reporting every guest

Once you are operating, two guest-reporting duties apply, and both happen at check-in, which is exactly when an owner abroad is least able to act.

  • TRA (Tarjeta de Registro de Alojamiento): MinCIT's guest registration card. The Alcaldía's guide for tourist homes lists implementing the TRA for every guest among the operator's obligations.
  • SIRE (Sistema de Información para el Reporte de Extranjeros): Migración Colombia's platform for reporting foreign nationals. Migración's ABC of SIRE includes accommodation that receives foreign tourists among those who must report. The reporting rules are set in Resolución 2357 de 2020, and the deadlines are short, so in practice someone has to collect each guest's passport details and file the report as soon as they arrive.

The city's guide also mentions other recurring duties, such as the quarterly parafiscal contribution to FONTUR and notifying the nearest police station. Missing any of these is a real risk: the Alcaldía has stepped up enforcement against tourist homes that operate illegally.

Money in and out: foreign investment and taxes

Two topics come up for almost every owner who lives abroad. We share general orientation only; for your own situation, consult a qualified Colombian accountant or lawyer.

Registering your foreign investment. When money from abroad is used to buy property in Colombia, it is normally channelled through the foreign-exchange market and registered with the Banco de la República. ProColombia's Invest in Colombia site has an overview of how to register a foreign investment in Colombia. Keeping that registration in order matters later, for example when you want to send sale proceeds back abroad or apply for certain visas.

Taxes on rental income. The DIAN, Colombia's tax authority, taxes non-residents on their Colombian-source income, and rent from a property in Colombia is Colombian-source income. DIAN guidance also addresses withholding on rent paid to non-residents (DIAN, Oficio 10721 de 2025), and whether you must file a Colombian return depends on your circumstances (DIAN Concepto 801 de 2024, via INCP). Your home country may tax the same income too. This is exactly where a Colombian accountant earns their fee.

Getting paid and staying informed

From abroad, the questions that matter most are simple: how much did the property earn, what did it cost, and when does the money reach me?

A few habits help:

  • Keep one place for every number. Booking income, platform fees, cleaning, utilities, building fees (administración) and repairs should all be recorded where you can see them.
  • Ask for proper monthly statements, not just a bank transfer. With us, owners get an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements.
  • Keep documents your accountant will ask for: contracts, invoices, platform payout reports and receipts.
  • Agree in writing how and when payouts happen, and how repair costs are approved.

When to bring in a property manager

You can do all of this yourself, but each item needs someone on the ground and on time: guest registration at every check-in, the annual RNT renewal, cleaning between stays, repairs, and a clear monthly report. That is the work professional property management in Medellín is built for. At Medellín Concierge we handle Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO management, dynamic pricing, 24/7 guest communication, RNT, SIRE and TRA registrations, cleaning and maintenance, long-term property management, and styling, photos and listings to launch your property, in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta. You can see our plans and fees at /#plans.

Own a property in Medellín and live abroad? Request a free consultation and we will walk you through what your apartment needs, as of today's rules.

FAQ

Can I rent my Medellín apartment on Airbnb while living outside Colombia?

Yes, foreign owners can rent to tourists, as long as the property meets the rules: an active RNT renewed every year, a building whose rules allow tourist use, compatible land use, and guest reporting through TRA and SIRE. Someone has to handle check-ins and reports locally, which is where a local manager helps. Requirements can change, so confirm them before you start.

Do I need to be in Colombia to register the RNT or file SIRE reports?

Registration is done online through the Confecámaras RNT system, and SIRE reports are filed on Migración Colombia's online platform. But the reports depend on each guest's arrival, so in practice you need someone in Medellín who can collect guest details and file on time.

Do foreign owners pay tax in Colombia on rental income?

The DIAN taxes non-residents on Colombian-source income, which includes rent from a property in Colombia, and withholding may apply. Whether you must file a return, and how your home country treats the income, depends on your situation. Consult a qualified Colombian accountant; we are not tax advisors.

item.title: How to Rent a Furnished Apartment in Medellín Without a Fiador
item.description: No Colombian co-signer? How to rent a furnished apartment in Medellín without a fiador: insurance, monthly rentals, deposit rules and a safety checklist.
item.content:encoded:
If you have looked for an apartment in Medellín for a few months, you have probably met the word fiador. Many Colombian landlords and rental agencies ask for one, and for a foreigner or a remote worker who just arrived, it can feel like a locked door. The good news: there are several legitimate ways to rent a furnished apartment in Medellín without a Colombian co-signer. This guide explains what a fiador is, what the usual alternatives are, which rules apply (as of November 2026), and what to check before you pay anything.

This is general information for renters, not legal advice. Rules and practices change, so confirm the details of any contract before you sign.

What is a fiador (or codeudor)?

A fiador or codeudor is a co-signer: a person who signs the lease with you and promises to pay if you don't. For traditional unfurnished leases, agencies often ask for a fiador who owns property in Colombia or has a verifiable local income. Colombia's residential lease law, Ley 820 de 2003, mentions co-debtors directly; for example, when a lease is written, the landlord must give a signed copy to the tenant and to any co-debtor.

For newcomers the problem is simple: you don't yet know anyone in Colombia who can sign for you. That is why the alternatives below matter.

Option 1: A rental insurance policy (póliza de arrendamiento)

Instead of a person, many landlords accept an insurance policy. A póliza de arrendamiento is an insurance product that protects the landlord if the tenant does not pay rent and related obligations such as building fees and utilities. The insurer reviews the applicant first, usually looking at income and credit history (El Espectador, La República).

What to know:

  • Approval depends on the insurer's review, which can be harder without a Colombian credit history.
  • Who pays for the policy is agreed in the contract, so ask before you sign.
  • The policy protects the landlord, not your belongings. If you want cover for your own things, that is a separate renter's insurance.

Option 2: Furnished monthly rentals from an owner or manager

Furnished apartments rented by the month, directly from an owner or a professional manager, are often the most practical route for travellers, remote workers and people who are still deciding where to live. These rentals are usually set up for people arriving from abroad: the apartment comes with furniture, kitchen equipment and internet, and the booking process is simpler than a traditional lease.

Requirements vary from one property to another, so always ask directly what is needed: identification, a signed contract, advance payment, or anything else. Don't assume that every furnished rental skips the fiador, and don't assume that every one requires it.

Option 3: Paying rent in advance

Some landlords accept advance rent instead of a co-signer, especially for shorter terms. If you go this way:

  • Put the agreement in a written contract that states how many months you prepaid and what happens if you leave early.
  • Pay by a traceable method and keep receipts.
  • Never prepay for an apartment you have not verified (see the checklist below).

What the law says about deposits (as of November 2026)

Here is something many renters don't know. For residential urban leases covered by Ley 820 de 2003, Article 16 prohibits requiring cash deposits or cauciones reales (collateral) to guarantee the contract, and the law sets sanctions for landlords who break this rule (Ley 820 de 2003). Article 15 allows a separate guarantee related to utility bills. In July 2026, Bogotá's housing authority published a legal opinion on how Articles 15 and 16 apply (Secretaría Distrital del Hábitat).

Whether a specific furnished or temporary rental falls under Ley 820 depends on how the contract is set up. If a deposit is requested, ask what it is for, how it is documented and when it is returned, and consult a qualified lawyer if you have doubts.

Short stays vs. monthly leases: the RNT

In Colombia, properties offered as tourist accommodation (vivienda turística) must be registered in the National Tourism Registry (RNT), and platforms remind hosts of this obligation (Airbnb Newsroom). Colombia's Superintendence of Industry and Commerce has said that the current definition of tourist housing does not rely on length of stay alone (SIC concept, April 2024).

For you as a renter, the practical takeaway is simple: for short stays, check that the listing shows an RNT number, and for monthly stays, make sure you receive a clear written contract.

Checklist before you pay anything

  1. Verify who you are dealing with. Ask for the owner's or company's name and confirm it. Anyone can request a property's certificado de tradición y libertad from the Superintendencia de Notariado y Registro to see who the registered owner is.
  2. See the apartment, in person or by live video call, not just photos.
  3. Get a written contract with the monthly price, what it includes (utilities, internet, building fees, cleaning), the dates, and the cancellation terms.
  4. Ask about the building's rules. Buildings in Colombia have a reglamento de propiedad horizontal that may affect guests, pets and moving in.
  5. Pay by a traceable method and keep every receipt.
  6. Document the inventory. Take photos of the furniture and condition on arrival.

Where to look

Start with listings where you can talk directly to the person responsible for the apartment and ask about requirements. You can browse our furnished rentals in Medellín and ask us what each apartment requires before you book.

If you own an apartment in Medellín and want to rent it to travellers and remote workers, our Medellín property management guide explains how professional property management in Medellín works.

FAQ

Can a foreigner rent an apartment in Medellín without a fiador?

Yes, it is possible. Common alternatives are a rental insurance policy (póliza de arrendamiento), a furnished monthly rental from an owner or manager, or an agreement to pay rent in advance. Requirements vary by property, so ask before you commit.

Is it legal for a landlord in Colombia to ask for a deposit?

For residential urban leases covered by Ley 820 de 2003, Article 16 prohibits requiring cash deposits or collateral, as of November 2026. Whether a specific furnished or temporary rental is covered depends on the contract. For a specific case, consult a qualified lawyer.

What should I check before paying for a furnished apartment in Medellín?

Confirm who owns or manages the property, see the apartment in person or by live video, get a written contract that lists what is included, check the building's rules, and pay only by a traceable method.

item.title: Airbnb Management in Medellín: What a Manager Does and What the Fees Cover
item.description: What an Airbnb manager or co-host in Medellín actually does, how management fees are usually structured, and what to ask before you sign. Updated Nov 2026.
item.content:encoded:
If you own an apartment in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado or Sabaneta and want to rent it on Airbnb, sooner or later you will ask the same question most owners ask: should I run it myself, or hand it to a manager? And if I hand it over, what exactly am I paying for?

This article explains what Airbnb management in Medellín usually includes, how managers and co-hosts are typically paid, how Airbnb's own fees fit in, and the questions worth asking before you sign anything. It is part of our Medellín property management guide, which covers short-term and long-term rentals in more depth.

This is general information as of November 2026, not legal or tax advice. Platform rules and Colombian regulations change, so confirm the current situation for your property with us before you act.

Manager or co-host: what is the difference?

On Airbnb, a co-host is a person or company the listing owner invites to help run a listing. Airbnb lets the owner choose what a co-host can access and, if they agree, pay the co-host directly through the platform (Airbnb Help Center: how co-host payouts work).

A property manager usually does the same work and more, often across several platforms (Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia, VRBO), and with responsibilities that go beyond the listing itself: cleaning teams, maintenance, building rules, registrations and owner reporting. In practice, many managers in Medellín also act as co-hosts on the owner's Airbnb account, so the two words overlap.

What matters is not the label but the scope: what will this person or company actually do, and what will stay on your plate?

What an Airbnb manager in Medellín typically does

A full-service manager normally takes care of the whole guest cycle:

  • Launching the listing. Styling, professional photos and a listing that describes the property honestly, so guests get what they expect.
  • Pricing. Adjusting nightly rates for seasons, holidays, events and demand. Medellín has busy periods around events such as the Feria de las Flores in August and the December holidays, and prices should move with them.
  • Guest communication, 24/7. Answering questions before booking, sending check-in instructions, and handling problems at any hour, in English and Spanish.
  • Check-in coordination. Working with the building's porter (portería) and administration so guests are registered and let in smoothly.
  • Cleaning and laundry. Turnovers between stays, linens and restocking basics.
  • Maintenance. Inspections, small repairs, and coordinating technicians when something breaks.
  • Compliance. Keeping the property's National Tourism Registry (RNT) up to date and reporting foreign guests through Migración Colombia's SIRE system. According to MinCIT, the RNT is free, done online and renewed every year between 1 January and 31 March. Migración Colombia operates SIRE for reporting foreign guests.
  • Reviews and reputation. Responding to reviews and fixing whatever guests repeatedly mention.
  • Money and reporting. Tracking income and expenses and sending the owner a clear statement every month.

At Medellín Concierge, owners also get an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements, so you can follow your property from wherever you live.

How Airbnb management fees are usually structured

There is no official or standard fee for managing an Airbnb in Medellín. Fees are agreed privately between the owner and the manager, and they vary with the scope of service, the property and the company. That is why it pays to understand the common structures before comparing offers.

Percentage of booking income

The most common model is a percentage of what each booking earns. Airbnb's own co-host tools reflect this: the owner can pay a co-host a percentage of each booking, a fixed amount, the cleaning fee, or the cleaning fee plus a percentage, and the payout is calculated from the host's earnings for each reservation (Airbnb Help Center).

When you compare percentages, always ask: a percentage of what? Gross booking value, earnings after Airbnb's fee, or earnings after cleaning? The same percentage can mean very different amounts.

Fixed monthly fee

Some managers charge a flat monthly amount instead. It is predictable, but it does not rise or fall with how well the property performs.

Setup and one-off costs

Launching a new listing can involve one-off costs: furniture and equipment, photography, and initial registrations. Ask which of these are included and which are billed separately.

What is usually billed on top

Even with management in place, the owner normally pays the property's own running costs: building administration fees, utilities, internet, supplies, repairs and taxes. Cleaning is often charged per stay, and frequently passed on to guests as a cleaning fee.

For our own plans and what each one includes, see our plans.

Do not forget Airbnb's own fee

The manager's fee is separate from what Airbnb charges. Airbnb has two structures: a split fee, where the host pays a small part and the guest pays a service fee, and a single fee paid entirely by the host (Airbnb Help Center: what are Airbnb service fees). In 2025 Airbnb moved most hosts, starting with those using property-management software, to the host-only fee; El Colombiano reported that hosts in Colombia now absorb a fee of about 15.5% that guests used to pay on top of the price.

In practice, this means the nightly rate you set has to cover Airbnb's fee, the manager's fee and your costs. A good manager will show you how they price with that in mind.

Questions to ask before you hire an Airbnb manager in Medellín

  1. What exactly is included? Get the list of services in writing, including who handles RNT renewal and SIRE reports.
  2. What is the fee based on? Gross bookings, net payout, or something else? Are cleaning fees included in the base?
  3. Who owns the listing and the reviews? Ideally the listing stays on your account and the manager is a co-host, so you keep your reviews if you ever change manager.
  4. How and when do I get paid? Ask how money flows, in which currency, and how often you receive statements.
  5. How are repairs approved? Is there a spending limit above which they need your approval?
  6. Can my building legally host short stays? Many buildings have rules in their reglamento de propiedad horizontal. Check before you invest in furnishing.
  7. What happens if I want to leave? Ask about notice periods and how future bookings are handled.

For tax questions, such as income tax on rental income or VAT on tourist accommodation, speak to a qualified Colombian tax professional. We are not tax advisors.

Is professional Airbnb management worth it?

It depends on your situation. If you live nearby, speak Spanish and enjoy hosting, you may prefer to run the listing yourself. If you live abroad, own several units or simply do not want calls at 2 a.m., a manager can take on the daily work while you keep visibility through reports.

If you want to talk it through, request a free consultation and we will look at your property, your building's rules and the options for property management in Medellín that fit you.

FAQ

How much does an Airbnb manager charge in Medellín?

There is no standard rate. Managers usually charge a percentage of booking income or a fixed monthly fee, and what is included varies widely. Compare offers by asking what the percentage is calculated on and what is billed separately. Our own plans are listed at /#plans.

Is a co-host the same as a property manager?

Not exactly. A co-host is someone the owner adds to an Airbnb listing to help run it. A property manager usually also handles cleaning teams, maintenance, multiple platforms, compliance and owner reporting, and often works as a co-host on the owner's account.

Who pays Airbnb's service fee?

As of November 2026, most hosts in Colombia are on Airbnb's single, host-only fee, which comes out of the host's payout (El Colombiano). Check your own listing settings, because Airbnb's fee structure can vary by listing and change over time.

item.title: Medellín Property Management: The Complete Guide for Owners
item.description: What Medellín property management covers: Airbnb vs long-term rentals, RNT and Law 820 rules, managing from abroad and how to choose a manager (Nov 2026).
item.content:encoded:
Owning an apartment in Medellín, Colombia, is the easy part. Keeping it rented, legal, well maintained and profitable, especially if you live in another country, is where most of the work is. This guide explains what Medellín property management actually covers, the two main ways to rent out a property (short-term and long-term), the rules that apply to each as of November 2026, and how to choose a manager you can trust.

It is written for owners and investors in El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta, whether you already own or are still shopping. It is general information, not legal or tax advice, and regulations change, so confirm the current rules for your property with us before you act.

What does a property manager in Medellín do?

A good manager takes over the day-to-day running of the property so the owner does not have to be in the city. Depending on the type of rental, that usually includes:

  • Getting the property ready. Furnishing and equipping an empty unit, professional photos, and a listing or advertisement that matches the property.
  • Finding guests or tenants. Publishing on Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO for short stays, or screening tenants for a long-term lease.
  • Pricing. Adjusting nightly rates for season, events and demand, or setting a monthly rent that fits the market and the law.
  • Communication. Answering guests around the clock, or being the tenant's single point of contact.
  • Cleaning and maintenance. Turnovers between stays, inspections, repairs and coordination with the building administration.
  • Compliance. Registrations and reports required by Colombian authorities (more on this below).
  • Money and reporting. Collecting income, paying building fees and utilities, and sending the owner a clear monthly statement.

At Medellín Concierge we handle this for you, with an owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements, so you can see what your property is doing without a phone call.

Short-term or long-term: the first decision

Most owners in Medellín choose between two models. Neither is "better"; the right one depends on your building, your goals and how hands-off you want to be.

Short-term rentals (vivienda turística)

Renting by the night or week to travellers through platforms like Airbnb. It usually involves more work (frequent cleaning, guest messages, pricing every day) and more regulation, but gives you flexibility to use the property yourself and adjust prices to demand.

In Colombia, a home rented to tourists is a vivienda turística, and it must be registered in the National Tourism Registry (RNT) before it operates. According to the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism (MinCIT), the RNT is free, is done online and must be renewed every year between 1 January and 31 March. On top of that, every stay must be reported through the TRA (MinCIT's accommodation registration card), foreign guests must be reported to Migración Colombia through SIRE, and, if the apartment is in a building under propiedad horizontal, the building's bylaws must allow tourist use.

The Alcaldía de Medellín has also stepped up inspections of informal tourist rentals, so compliance is not optional.

Long-term rentals (arriendo de vivienda)

Renting to one tenant for months or years under a lease. There is less day-to-day work and no guest turnover, but less flexibility, and the lease is governed by Law 820 of 2003, the national law on urban housing leases. Two points every owner should know:

  • Rent cap. Article 18 says the monthly rent cannot exceed 1% of the property's commercial value (and that estimated value cannot exceed twice the official cadastral value).
  • Annual increases. Article 20 allows the owner to raise the rent once every 12 months, by no more than the previous year's consumer price inflation (IPC), as long as the new rent stays within the Article 18 cap.

The law also covers deposits, contract renewals, termination notices and eviction procedures, which is why most foreign owners prefer a local manager to handle the lease.

Furnished mid-term stays

Between the two sits a growing middle ground: furnished stays of one month or more for remote workers and professionals. These can mean fewer turnovers than nightly rentals, but the right legal and contractual setup depends on how the stay is structured. Ask us before you switch models.

The rules for managers themselves

In Colombia, people and companies that rent out homes on behalf of others, or act as intermediaries between owners and tenants, must be registered with the local authority. In Medellín this is the matrícula de arrendadores, a procedure handled by the Alcaldía. It exists under Law 820 of 2003 so the city can supervise rental intermediaries. When you compare managers for long-term rentals, asking about this registration is a simple and reasonable check.

Managing your property from abroad

Many owners of property in Medellín live abroad. Owning from abroad is entirely possible, but plan for a few extra things:

  • Someone on the ground. Leaks, lost keys and building meetings do not wait for your next visit.
  • Banking and payments. Building fees (administración), utilities and property tax (predial) must be paid on time in Colombian pesos.
  • Foreign investment registration. Foreign owners usually need their investment properly registered with the Banco de la República (generally done through the foreign-exchange declaration when the funds come in through an authorized bank), so they can later take money out of the country. Ask your lawyer or advisor how this applies to your purchase.
  • Taxes. Rental income from Colombian property is generally taxable in Colombia. For non-residents, DIAN guidance (for example Oficio 2179 of 2019) explains that withholding tax and filing duties depend on the specific situation. You may also have obligations in your home country. Get advice from a qualified tax professional; we are not tax advisors.

How to choose a property manager in Medellín

Whether you are comparing inmobiliarias, Airbnb co-hosts or full-service companies, these questions help:

  1. What exactly is included? Listing, pricing, cleaning, maintenance, guest messages, compliance, reporting. Get it in writing.
  2. How are fees structured? Percentage of income, fixed fee, or a mix, and which costs (cleaning, supplies, repairs) are charged separately.
  3. Who handles RNT, TRA and SIRE? For short-term rentals this should be a clear yes.
  4. Are they registered? For long-term leases, ask about the matrícula de arrendadores.
  5. How will you see your numbers? Monthly statements, an owner portal, access to booking data.
  6. What areas do they really know? Rules, demand and buildings differ between El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado and Sabaneta.
  7. What does the contract say about leaving? Notice periods and how your listing and data are handed back.

Where Medellín Concierge fits

We offer full property management in Medellín for both models: Airbnb, Booking.com, Expedia and VRBO management with smart pricing and 24/7 guest communication; RNT, SIRE and TRA registrations; cleaning and maintenance; long-term property management; and styling, photos and listings to launch your property. Owners follow everything through the owner portal and monthly GAAP financial statements.

This guide is the hub of our owner series. In the coming weeks we will go deeper into Airbnb management, long-term rentals, managing from abroad and each neighborhood. If you would rather talk it through now, request a free consultation and we will look at your property, your building rules and the model that suits you.

FAQ

How much does property management cost in Medellín?

It varies by model and scope. Short-term management is usually priced as a percentage of rental income, and long-term management as a percentage of the monthly rent, with cleaning and repairs often billed separately. Ask any manager for a written breakdown. Our own fees are published on our plans page, and we are happy to walk you through them in a free consultation.

Can a foreigner own and rent out property in Medellín?

Yes. Foreigners can buy property in Colombia and rent it out. The same rules apply as for Colombians (RNT and guest reporting for short stays, Law 820 of 2003 for long leases), plus foreign investment registration and tax duties that depend on your residency.

Is short-term or long-term rental better in Medellín?

It depends on whether your building allows tourist use, how much involvement you want and how you plan to use the property. A manager can compare both options for your specific unit before you commit.
